lead: A dryer design is three balances and two sizing rules. The water balance gives the kg of water to remove each hour. The air balance gives the kg of dry air that carries it. The heat balance gives the fuel or steam duty. Then the air mass velocity fixes the diameter, and a length-to-diameter ratio fixes the length. That is how rotary dryers for sand, fertiliser, detergents and clay are sized before any drawing is made.
prereq: You need: 7.1 for humidity and humid volume, 7.7 for drying time, and 7.8 for dryer types.

sections.h3: Water balance, air balance, heat duty

blocks.text: Start with the bone-dry solid S, kg/h. It does not change. The feed carries water W₁ kg/h and the product carries W₂ kg/h. The water evaporated is W = W₁ − W₂. Moisture is usually given on a wet basis, so convert: dry-basis ratio X = x/(1 − x), where x is the wet-basis mass fraction.
W = S × [x₁/(1 − x₁) − x₂/(1 − x₂)] = F·x₁ − P·x₂, or W = S(X₁ − X₂)
blocks.where: W is water evaporated, kg/h; S is bone-dry solid, kg/h; F and P are wet feed and product, kg/h; x₁ and x₂ are wet-basis mass fractions; X₁ and X₂ are dry-basis kg water per kg dry solid.

blocks.text: The dry air carries that water: mₐ = W/(Y₂ − Y₁), where mₐ is kg dry air/h and Y is kg water per kg dry air. A small humidity rise means a huge air flow and a fat shell. A large rise means the outlet air is near saturation and the solids may re-wet. Keep outlet air below about 80 % relative humidity.

Useful heat has three parts: evaporate water, heat the solids, heat the water left in the product. Total fuel duty comes from the air-side balance mₐ(h_in − h_amb)/η, which includes shell losses. Drying efficiency = W·λ/Q_fuel, typically 40 to 70 % for a direct rotary dryer.
Q_useful = W·λ + S·cₚₛ·(T₂ − T₁) + W₂·cₚw·(T₂ − T₁)
blocks.where: Q_useful is useful heat, kJ/h; λ is latent heat at the wet-bulb temperature, about 2400 kJ/kg; cₚₛ is specific heat of dry solid, kJ/(kg·K); cₚw is 4.18 kJ/(kg·K); T₁ and T₂ are solid inlet and outlet temperatures, °C.

blocks.text: A rotary dryer is a slightly inclined cylinder, 0.5° to 5° to the horizontal, turning at 1 to 8 rpm. Wet feed enters one end, tumbles down the shell, meets hot air, and leaves dry at the other end. Two empirical numbers fix the geometry.

items: Get mₐ in kg/s from the water balance and the allowed humidity rise.
Choose air mass velocity G, usually 1.5 to 2.5 kg/(m²·s) on the empty shell cross-section. Higher G means smaller diameter but more dust carry-over and fan power.
Cross-section A = mₐ/G, then diameter D = √(4A/π). Round up to a standard shell size.
Pick L/D between 4 and 10. Take L = 6D for a typical case.
Check residence time, roughly 5 to 120 min. It must exceed the drying time from the rate curve in 7.7.
Compute heat duty and efficiency. Check outlet air temperature against the solid's tolerance.

blocks.text: Fan volumetric flow uses humid volume at the outlet: v_H = (1/29 + Y/18) × 22.4 × (T + 273)/273 m³/kg dry air. Multiply by mₐ, never by total humid air mass. Air cools and gains water, so the outlet humid volume is usually smaller than the hot inlet volume. Size the exhaust fan on outlet conditions.

sections.h3: Flights inside the shell, and flow arrangement

blocks.text: Inside the shell are longitudinal fins called flights. As the shell turns, a flight lifts a wedge of solids and showers it through the hot gas. Most heat and mass transfer happens in that shower. Spiral flights at the feed end move wet sticky solids in quickly. Straight flights in the middle give a full curtain. Short flights near discharge stop dusting.

In cocurrent, air and solids move the same way. The hottest gas meets the wettest solid, so heat-sensitive materials such as PVC and soap are safe. But the exhaust gas leaves warmer than in counter-current, so more sensible heat is lost and thermal efficiency is lower. In counter-current the dry solid meets the hottest gas, giving the best heat economy and the driest product, but the solid must tolerate the high outlet temperature. Rule: heat-sensitive solid, cocurrent; fuel cost matters, counter-current.

Use a rotary dryer for free-flowing granular solids, not for pastes that ball up. For pastes, use a drum dryer or another paste-capable dryer; spray dryers suit pumpable solutions and slurries. See 7.8.

figure.caption: The design chain for a rotary dryer: the water balance sets the air rate, the air rate sets the diameter, and the length and heat duty follow. Each box needs only the box before it.

spec.title: Sizing a rotary dryer
spec.aria: A five-step vertical chain: water evaporated, dry air rate, shell diameter, shell length, then heat duty and efficiency.

examples.question: A rotary dryer treats 1000 kg/h of wet solid at 25 % moisture (wet basis) and delivers it at 2 % moisture (wet basis). Air enters at Y = 0.010 kg water/kg dry air and leaves at Y = 0.035. The air mass velocity is 2.0 kg/(m²·s) and L/D = 6. Find the water evaporated, the dry air rate, the shell diameter and the shell length.
steps: Product is 98 % solid, so P = 750/0.98 = 765.3 kg/h and W₂ = 765.3 − 750 = 15.3 kg/h.
Humidity rise: Y₂ − Y₁ = 0.035 − 0.010 = 0.025 kg water/kg dry air.
Dry air rate: mₐ = 234.7/0.025 = 9388 kg dry air/h = 2.608 kg/s.
Heat for evaporation alone: Q = 234.7 × 2400 = 5.63 × 10⁵ kJ/h.
examples.answer: Water evaporated 234.7 kg/h, dry air 9388 kg/h (2.61 kg/s), shell diameter 1.3 m, shell length 7.8 m.
examples.check:
S = 1000*(1-0.25)
W1 = 1000*0.25
P = S/0.98
W2 = P - S
W = W1 - W2
print(round(W,1))
ma_h = W/(0.035-0.010)
print(round(ma_h))
ma = ma_h/3600
print(round(ma,3))
A = ma/2.0
print(round(A,3))
import math
D = math.sqrt(4*A/math.pi)
print(round(D,3))
Dstd = 1.3
L = 6*Dstd
print(round(L,1))
Q = W*2400
print(round(Q))

examples.question: For the same dryer, the solids enter at 25 °C and leave at 70 °C. The dry solid has cₚₛ = 1.2 kJ/(kg·K). Find the useful heat duty (kJ/h) and the fraction used for evaporation.
steps: Heat to raise dry solid: Q₂ = 750 × 1.2 × (70 − 25) = 40 500 kJ/h.
Heat to raise remaining water: Q₃ = 15.3 × 4.18 × 45 = 2878 kJ/h.
Fraction of useful heat used for evaporation = Q₁/Q_useful = 0.929, that is 92.9 %. This is not the dryer efficiency.
Drying efficiency = W·λ/Q_fuel. Get Q_fuel from the air-side balance; it is typically 40 to 70 %.
examples.answer: Useful heat duty about 606 700 kJ/h; 92.9 % of it goes to evaporation. Dryer efficiency needs the fuel duty from the air side.
examples.check:
W = 234.7
W2 = 15.3
S = 750
Q1 = W*2400
Q2 = S*1.2*(70-25)
Q3 = W2*4.18*(70-25)
Q = Q1+Q2+Q3
print(round(Q1))
print(round(Q2))
print(round(Q3))
print(round(Q))
print(round(Q1/Q,3))

traps: Using wet-basis percentage as kg water per kg dry solid. Convert before the balance.
Using total humid air mass instead of dry air mass in the volumetric flow, so the fan is oversized.
Forgetting sensible heat for solids and remaining moisture; the duty comes out too low and the air heater is undersized.
Taking fan volumetric flow at inlet temperature. Air cools and gains water; the outlet humid volume is usually smaller than the hot inlet volume, so using inlet T oversizes the fan.
Mixing up cocurrent and counter-current: cocurrent protects heat-sensitive solids but its exhaust gas leaves warmer, so thermal efficiency is lower.

quiz.q: What is the usual range of air mass velocity in a rotary dryer, and what does it fix?
quiz.a: 1.5 to 2.5 kg/(m²·s) on the empty shell cross-section. It fixes the shell diameter.

quiz.q: State the typical length-to-diameter ratio of a rotary dryer shell.
quiz.a: About 4 to 10; L/D = 6 is a common first choice.

quiz.q: Why does cocurrent operation suit a heat-sensitive solid?
quiz.a: The hottest gas meets the wettest solid, so evaporative cooling keeps the solid surface near the wet-bulb temperature. The solid never meets gas hotter than it can take.

quiz.q: Why is the drying efficiency less than 100 % even with no shell losses?
quiz.a: Part of the heat raises the dry solid and remaining moisture to outlet temperature, and part leaves with the warm exhaust air. Only latent heat of evaporated water counts as useful.

quiz.q: A dryer must evaporate 150 kg/h of water using air from Y = 0.008 to Y = 0.030. Find the dry air rate in kg/s.
For that 1.894 kg/s air and G = 2.0 kg/(m²·s), find the diameter.
A plant raises the air mass velocity from 1.5 to 2.5 kg/(m²·s) at the same air flow. What happens to the shell and to product quality, and what limits how far you can go?
quiz.a: Diameter falls by √(1.5/2.5) = 0.775, so about 22 % smaller, and cost falls. But higher gas velocity carries more fines into the cyclone, and pressure drop and fan power rise. The limit is dust carry-over and fan power, not the mass balance.

quiz.q: Your product leaves at 3 % moisture instead of the target 2 %. Air rate and temperatures are at design. List two likely causes inside the shell and the fix for each.
quiz.a: Residence time too short, from too steep a slope, too high an rpm, or overloading; fix by decreasing slope or rpm, or lowering feed rate. Or flights are worn or wrongly arranged, so the curtain is poor and gas bypasses; fix by replacing or re-arranging the flights.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industrial rotary dryers are now often modelled with CFD to check the flight curtain. Heat-pump dryers recover latent heat from the exhaust and reach high efficiencies for low-temperature food and timber drying. Solar dryers suit small farms, and waste-heat recovery from kiln or boiler flue gas is common in cement and fertiliser plants.
